issues.description: The study measures 'causal understanding' using a 10-item forced-choice prediction task about which of two wheels will be faster. This measures predictive knowledge of specific configurations, not necessarily the underlying causal mechanisms or mental models of the participants.
issues.quote: Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to predict which wheel would reach the bottom of the rails first.

issues.description: The study lacks a baseline control group where individuals perform the task for 25 trials without social transmission. Without this, it is impossible to definitively attribute the optimization to cultural accumulation rather than just extended individual trial-and-error learning over the same total number of trials.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain so as to simulate overlapping generations.

issues.description: The authors deviated from their preregistered analysis plan because their model did not converge. They chose to aggregate the scores for inertia and center of mass into a single score. This post-hoc analytic choice obscures the multidimensional nature of the understanding they originally intended to measure.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.description: Assigning a speed of 0 to wheels that did not descend creates a zero-inflated distribution. A failure to descend is a qualitatively different outcome (infinite time) than a slow descent. Including these as 0s in a linear model violates distributional assumptions and artificially skews the means and variances.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.
issues.location: Methods / Statistical analyses and models output

issues.description: The experimenter, who physically positioned the weights on the wheel based on the participant's input, was not blind to the experimental conditions. This introduces a significant risk of experimenter bias, especially in how the wheel was released or how failures were recorded.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: Extrapolation from low-dimensional toy task to complex technology
issues.description: The authors make broad claims about the evolution of complex, high-dimensional human technologies (like bows and kayaks) based on a highly constrained, 2-dimensional physics toy task. The cognitive requirements for a 2-variable problem are vastly different from those required for real-world technological innovation.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.description: The requirement that theories must be under 340 characters and start with a specific prompt artificially constrains how participants can express their causal models. This may lead to an underestimation of their actual explicit understanding.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.subcategory: Reporting models with poor MCMC sampling
issues.description: The authors report Analysis 3 despite acknowledging that the chains were inefficient and the effective sample size for a parameter was low. While they ran additional models, the primary reported model in the text should be one that meets standard convergence and sampling diagnostics.
issues.quote: For this model, the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low (see Supplementary Table 3).
issues.location: Methods / Statistical analyses and models output

issues.description: The text reports a mean understanding score of -0.04 with a CI of (-0.34, 0.25) for the Generation effect, but then immediately states the first generation score was 4.60 and the fifth generation was 4.47. It is unclear how the model estimates (-0.04) relate to the raw scores (4.60), likely due to unstated centering or scaling.
issues.quote: participants’ understanding did not (Generation 95% CI: (-0.34, 0.25), mean = -0.04, Figure 2.B). The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h... and their understanding score was 4.60

issues.description: Participants are paid based on the next participant's performance. In the Theory condition, they can actively help the next person by writing a good theory. In the Configurations condition, they can only 'help' by producing good configurations. This difference in affordances to cooperate might alter their exploration strategies independently of cultural transmission dynamics.
issues.quote: Participants were informed that their last two trials would be transmitted to the next participant in the chain, and that their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain.

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from non-randomized theory inheritance
issues.description: The authors claim that inheriting a specific theory causes changes in exploration and understanding. However, the theory a participant inherits is not randomly assigned; it is generated by the previous participant. Unobserved chain-level characteristics could drive both the type of theory generated and the subsequent exploration behavior.
issues.quote: Finally, we show that the transmission of these inaccurate theories constrains learners’ exploration and has downstream effects on their understanding.

issues.subcategory: Insufficient demographic details on educational background
issues.description: The study involves a physics optimization task, yet the authors only report age and sex in the main demographics. They mention asking about physics/engineering backgrounds at the end, but do not report the distribution of these backgrounds across the experimental conditions, which could act as a major confound.
issues.quote: The subjects ranged in age from 18 to 38 y (mean of 20.5, SD of 3.4).

issues.subcategory: Conflation of explicit theory with causal reasoning
issues.description: The authors equate the inability to articulate a correct, multidimensional written theory with a lack of 'causal understanding.' However, participants demonstrated non-random, highly directed exploration, suggesting they possessed implicit causal models. The theoretical framework conflates explicit verbalization with causal reasoning.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.description: Participants are only given 5 trials to optimize a system with 20,736 possible configurations. This is an extremely short window for individual learning. The failure to develop accurate causal models may simply be an artifact of not having enough time to explore the system, rather than a fundamental limitation of human causal reasoning.
issues.quote: Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track.

issues.description: In Analyses 1 and 3, the authors restrict the data to the participants' last two trials to 'limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend.' Discarding 60% of the trial data is an arbitrary and massive exclusion that removes critical information about the learning and exploration process.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.
issues.location: Methods / Statistical analyses and models output

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous response options in understanding test
issues.description: The understanding test includes a 'No difference' option. If the 10 pairs of wheels always had a physically faster option, 'No difference' is always incorrect. Including it changes the probability of guessing correctly from 50% to 33%, and might confuse participants who think it's a trick question.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

issues.subcategory: Unclear inter-rater reliability metric for 5 raters
issues.description: The authors report 'Cohen’s kappa coefficients' for 5 raters. Cohen's kappa is designed for exactly two raters. It is unclear if they used Fleiss' kappa, an average of pairwise Cohen's kappas, or something else. This makes it impossible to properly evaluate the reliability of the theory coding.
issues.quote: Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.description: Participants in the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment receive more information to process between trials than those in the 'Configurations' treatment. This increased cognitive load, especially within a short 5-trial window, could interfere with their ability to optimize the wheel, confounding the effect of theory transmission.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.subcategory: Absence of evidence interpreted as evidence of absence
issues.description: The authors conclude that theory transmission has 'no noticeable effect' based on the credible intervals for the treatment effect crossing zero. They do not provide a formal equivalence test or Bayes Factor to quantify evidence for the null hypothesis, making the strong claim of 'no effect' statistically unsupported.
issues.quote: Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: The authors claim an 'optimization of 71%' but the math is not transparent. With a max speed of 154, a starting speed of 123.6, and an ending speed of 145.7, the improvement is 22.1 out of a possible 30.4, which is ~72.7%. The discrepancy or the exact formula used to derive 71% is not explained.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: The study uses chains of only 5 individuals to model cultural evolution. Real-world cultural accumulation occurs over dozens or hundreds of generations. It is highly possible that accurate multidimensional causal theories would emerge and prove beneficial in longer chains, making the 5-generation limit a severe threat to the study's conclusions.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals.

issues.description: The authors frequently mention wheels that 'did not descend' or 'failures', but they never explicitly define the physical criteria for a failure. Did the wheel get stuck? Did it roll backwards? Without a strict operational definition, the recording of failures is subject to experimenter interpretation.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment.

issues.description: The authors state that the cultural niche hypothesis predicts understanding will not improve over generations. This is a mischaracterization; the hypothesis posits that understanding is not necessary for improvement, but it does not preclude understanding from increasing alongside technological optimization.
issues.quote: The cultural niche hypothesis predicts that the speed of the wheel will increase with generations, while participants’ understanding of the system will not improve over generations (preregistered hypothesis 1).

issues.description: The payoff formula uses a MinSpeed of 96. It is not explained what happens if a wheel descends but records a speed lower than 96. Does the participant receive a negative payoff? Is 96 the absolute physical minimum? This lack of detail obscures the actual incentive structure.
issues.quote: with MaxSpeed = 160, MinSpeed = 96. RecordedSpeed was the recorded average speed of the wheel.

issues.description: The authors explicitly state that chains were 'exclusively males or exclusively females' but provide absolutely no theoretical or methodological justification for this design choice, nor do they include sex as a variable in their analyses.
issues.quote: In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.description: The models include 'Chain's identity' as a random intercept, but this does not account for the autoregressive nature of the data within a chain (Generation 3 depends on Generation 2). Failing to model this sequential dependency violates the assumption of independence of residuals within clusters.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable, “Generation” as a predictor variable and “Chain’s identity” as a random effect
issues.location: Methods / Statistical analyses and models output

issues.subcategory: Overstated ecological validity of the experimental task
issues.description: The authors claim the task has high ecological validity because it uses real physics. However, the highly constrained, discrete nature of the wheel (12 notches, 4 spokes) is entirely artificial and lacks the continuous, multi-material complexity of real-world technological design, undermining the ecological validity claim.
issues.quote: Second, the performance of the wheel depends solely on the laws of physics, and not on arbitrary principles that could compromise the ecological validity of our results.

issues.subcategory: Missing details on the difficulty of understanding test items
issues.description: The 10 pairs of wheels used in the understanding test are not described in the main text. Without knowing how subtle or extreme the differences between the paired wheels were, it is impossible to evaluate whether the test was too difficult (floor effect) or too easy, which directly impacts the interpretation of the understanding scores.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: Confounding of exploration behavior and implicit understanding
issues.description: The authors argue that producing balanced wheels caused participants to understand inertia better (a canalizing effect). However, the reverse is equally plausible: participants who implicitly understood inertia chose to build balanced wheels. The correlational data cannot distinguish between these causal directions.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: Undisclosed criteria for categorizing exploration behavior
issues.description: In the exploratory analysis, participants are grouped into those who produced 'various types', 'only balanced', or 'only unbalanced' wheels. The specific mathematical or physical thresholds used to define these categories are not disclosed, introducing significant researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: we grouped participants who did not inherit any theory (i.e. from the “Configurations” treatment) into 3 categories: those who produced various types of wheels, those who only produced balanced wheels, and those who only produced unbalanced wheels.
